extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, evolutionary_biologists, and students of anthropology/natural history
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and lines of evidence Darwin uses to judge whether sexual selection has acted on human traits (and when it will be inhibited). Useful for evaluating hypotheses about mate-choice driven evolution in humans and related animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that choice is exerted before parents unite
rubrics_metrics.description: “All that is required is that choice should be exerted before the parents unite, and it signifies little whether the unions last for life or only for a season.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sexual selection operates only when mating choices are made prior to pair formation; temporary pairings (e.g., per-birth unions) can still permit sexual selection. Emphasize timing of mate preference rather than duration of the union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communal marriage / promiscuous intercourse prevents sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: If pairing is left to mere chance with no choice exerted by either sex, there can be no sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extreme licentiousness or communal marriage (all men and women husbands/wives to one another) eliminates differential reproductive success based on mate choice. Darwin cites Sir J. Lubbock, M’Lennan and Morgan as sources claiming such systems existed or were ancestral, but notes that evidence for absolute promiscuity is doubtful. Use ethnographic data on mating exclusivity to assess whether sexual selection could act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female infanticide reduces the strength of sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Where infanticide (especially of females) prevails, the struggle for existence is less severe and women become scarce, altering mating patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Female infanticide lessens competition among offspring and can create sex-ratio imbalances that lead to wife-capture, exogamy, or polyandry — all of which alter or inhibit mate-choice-based selection. Examples: Azara (South America), Ellis (Polynesia), MacCulloch (India). Consider demographic impacts when evaluating sexual-selection hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early betrothals and arranged marriages prevent selection by appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Betrothing females while infants would prevent preference being exerted on either side according to personal appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mate partners are fixed early by parents/tribal arrangements, individual aesthetic choice is curtailed. However, attractive individuals might still be stolen or later reselected by powerful men; ethnographic nuance matters (check reports of wife-capture, elopement, post-betrothal choice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Low estimation / slavery of women curtails sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: When women are valued merely as slaves/beasts of burden, men's ability or incentive to select on beauty is reduced, though men may still prefer the handsomest slaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social status and autonomy of women influence the direction and intensity of sexual selection. Evaluate the degree of female agency and commodification in a society to predict selection dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polyandry prevents male-driven selection but can enable female choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever two or more men marry one woman, all the women of the tribe will get married and there will be no selection by the men of the more attractive women; women, however, may have the power of choice and prefer the more attractive men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different mating systems change which sex exercises selection. In polyandrous contexts, expect selection pressure on men via female choice; in polygynous contexts expect selection on women via male choice. Use ethnographic mating system data to infer which sex is the primary selector.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential reproductive success of powerful men amplifies sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The strongest and most vigorous men — those who could best defend and hunt, who had best weapons and property — would succeed in rearing a greater average number of offspring and would generally be able to select the more attractive women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sexual selection is effective when mate preference correlates with variance in reproductive success. Evidence such as chiefs obtaining multiple wives (examples: New Zealand, Kafirs) indicates how leaders can impose a selective filter. Quantify reproductive skew to assess potential strength of sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-tribe mating (exogamy, capture, barter) and gene flow reduce differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Incessant crossing between tribe and tribe tends to keep people in the same country nearly uniform in character, interfering with sexual selection's power to differentiate tribes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High gene flow and recurrent intermarriage homogenize populations, preventing local standards of beauty from producing divergent evolutionary outcomes. Consider rates of exogamy and historical practices (capture, bride-purchase) when predicting divergence due to sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation and emergence of different standards of beauty enable divergent sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: If isolated hordes develop slightly different conditions and habits, each isolated tribe would form for itself a slightly different standard of beauty, and unconscious selection would come into action through the powerful preferring certain women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Population subdivision plus cultural divergence in aesthetic norms allows sexual selection to magnify small differences. Look for cultural isolation, barriers to gene flow, and diverging aesthetic preferences as preconditions for divergence by sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy to unconscious/artificial selection as evidence of mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: When breeders rear animals without comparing them, after generations they become slightly different—each breeder has impressed 'the character of his own mind' on his animals; similar unconscious selection by preferred mates can operate in human tribes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies from domestication and unconscious selection to argue plausibility: consistent mate preferences over generations (even without explicit intent) can shift trait frequencies. Empirical support can come from longitudinal or comparative cultural data showing stable aesthetic preferences and their reproductive consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female choice can produce male ornaments and influence sexual dimorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: When females are the selectors and accept only those males which charm them most, ornamental characters are acquired by males; conversely, when females have been long selected for beauty they may transmit ornamentation to female offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine which sex exercises preference to predict direction of ornament evolution. Darwin gives ethnographic examples of women exercising choice (running away to lovers, rejecting parental matches) across many peoples (e.g., Patagonians, Fuegians, Kalmucks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance pattern (sex-limited vs shared transmission) affects outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some successive variations may be transmitted exclusively or chiefly to the same sex, so that ornamental characters can be transmitted predominantly to females (or males) and affect sexual dimorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a trait evolved via sexual selection, consider whether the trait's genetic/inheritance pattern is sex-limited or expressed in both sexes. Examples: traits transmitted mainly to female offspring could make women more ornamented than men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of hair on the body plausibly attributed to sexual selection when natural selection/climate explanations fail
rubrics_metrics.description: No one supposes nakedness of the skin is any direct advantage to man; his body cannot have been divested of hair through natural selection or climate alone—therefore hairlessness may be a secondary sexual character gained through sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a putative adaptive explanation (climate, natural selection) is implausible, sexual selection is a candidate cause. Use developmental evidence (lanugo on the foetus, rudimentary hairs) and sexual dimorphism (women less hairy than men) as supporting lines of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jealousy and male combat provide a mechanism analogous to other animals
rubrics_metrics.description: From the jealousy of all male quadrupeds and the presence of special weapons for battling rivals, promiscuous intercourse in a state of nature is extremely improbable; mate-guarding and male contests have contributed to sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioural analogies (male jealousy, contests for mates) support expectations about which traits are selected (strength, weapons, pugnacity). Examine comparative ethology (quadrumana and other mammals) for parallels when inferring sexual-selection processes in humans.
